**Arnolfini Portrait (Arnolfini Wedding)**
Van Eyck's 1434 double portrait of the Italian merchant Giovanni Arnolfini, in a dark cloak and a large black hat, holding the hand of his wife, who wears a green dress and only appears to be pregnant. Famous details include oranges on the windowsill, a brass chandelier with a single lit candle, a small dog, and discarded wooden pattens (clogs). Erwin Panofsky famously argued that the painting served as a visual marriage certificate.

**Convex mirror and "Johannes de eyck fuit hic 1434"**
On the back wall of the Arnolfini Portrait hangs a convex mirror that reflects the backs of the couple and two figures in the doorway, one possibly the artist himself. Its frame holds tiny roundels of scenes from the Passion of Christ. Above it, van Eyck wrote in elaborate script "Jan van Eyck was here 1434."

**Ghent Altarpiece**
A huge polyptych of twelve panels, painted on both sides, in St. Bavo's Cathedral in Ghent. It was begun by Jan's brother Hubert and completed by Jan in 1432 for the patron Joos Vijd and his wife Elisabeth Borluut.

**Adoration of the Mystic Lamb**
The central lower panel of the Ghent Altarpiece. The Lamb of God stands on an altar, bleeding from its chest into a chalice, while angels kneel around it. Crowds representing Old and New Testament figures, saints, and martyrs gather on all sides, and below it the Fountain of Life feeds a small stream.

**God the Father, singing angels, and Adam and Eve**
The upper register of the open Ghent Altarpiece. It shows an enthroned figure in a jeweled red robe and a papal triple crown, usually read as God the Father or Christ, flanked by Mary, John the Baptist, singing angels, and an angel playing an organ. Nude figures of Adam and Eve stand in niches at the far ends, with small scenes of Cain killing Abel above them.

**Exterior of the Ghent Altarpiece**
When the altarpiece is closed, it shows the donors Joos Vijd and Elisabeth Borluut kneeling before grisaille (gray, stone-like) imitation statues of St. John the Baptist and St. John the Evangelist. Above them is an Annunciation in which Mary's reply, "Ecce ancilla Domini," is painted upside down, so that it can be read from heaven.

**"Just Judges" panel and the Monuments Men**
The Ghent Altarpiece is often called the most stolen artwork in history. Its lower-left "Just Judges" panel was stolen in 1934 and has never been recovered. The Nazis seized the altarpiece during World War II, and the Monuments Men recovered it from the Altaussee salt mine in Austria and returned it to Ghent.

**"Als ich can" ("As I can")**
Van Eyck's personal motto, a modest pun on his own name ("ich"/"Eyck"). He inscribed it on the frames of several paintings, sometimes in Greek letters, including the Man in a Red Turban and the portrait of his wife Margaret.

**Madonna of Chancellor Rolin**
A painting showing Nicolas Rolin, chancellor of the Duchy of Burgundy, kneeling in prayer before the Virgin Mary. An angel holds a crown over her head, and the infant Christ blesses Rolin while holding a crystal globe topped with a cross. Behind the loggia, peacocks walk along a balcony overlooking a detailed river city and landscape.

**Virgin and Child with Canon van der Paele**
A 1436 painting in which St. George lifts his helmet to present the elderly canon Joris van der Paele, in a white surplice and holding a book and spectacles, to the Virgin and Child. St. Donatian stands on the other side.

**Man in a Red Turban**
A 1433 portrait, widely believed to be a self-portrait, of a man wearing an elaborately folded red chaperon, a headdress often mistaken for a turban. Its frame carries the motto "Als ich can."

**Portrait of Margaret van Eyck**
A 1439 portrait of the artist's wife, wearing a red dress and a horned headdress. Its frame is inscribed with his motto and a note that her husband Jan completed the painting.

**New York Diptych (Crucifixion and Last Judgment)**
A pair of tall panels attributed to van Eyck and his workshop, now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. In the Last Judgment panel, the archangel Michael stands on the back of a huge, bat-winged skeleton representing Death, which spreads over the damned in Hell.

**Lucca Madonna**
A painting of the Virgin nursing the Christ Child on a canopied throne decorated with four small lions, in a richly detailed interior. It is named after a former owner, the Duke of Lucca.

**Myth of inventing oil painting**
The Renaissance biographer Giorgio Vasari wrongly credited van Eyck with inventing oil paint. Van Eyck did not invent it, but his mastery of thin, layered oil glazes produced unprecedented detail and luminosity and made him the leading figure of Early Netherlandish painting.
